title: Headache: the red flags, and treating the common ones

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the SNNOOP10 red-flag framework, the International Classification of Headache Disorders, and the American Headache Society treatment guidance. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: Which headache features are red flags that need urgent investigation?
a: Sudden onset reaching maximum within a minute
A change in the usual pattern
Headache brought on by exertion or Valsalva
questions.why: Systemic symptoms, a history of cancer or HIV, a neurological deficit, positional headache, pregnancy, and post-traumatic onset complete the list. The distractors are ordinary migraine.

questions.q: A thunderclap headache. Within how many hours of onset does a normal non-contrast CT effectively exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage?
questions.why: After six hours the sensitivity falls and a lumbar puncture, looking for xanthochromia, or a CT angiogram is needed. Thunderclap means the worst headache of life peaking within a minute.

questions.q: A 72-year-old has a new temporal headache, jaw pain on chewing, and a raised ESR. What is done first?
questions.a: Start high-dose corticosteroids now, before the biopsy
d: Wait for the temporal artery biopsy
Arrange an MRI in a week
questions.why: Giant cell arteritis blinds if untreated. The biopsy stays diagnostic for a couple of weeks after steroids start, so treatment never waits for it.

questions.q: An obese young woman with headache and papilloedema has a normal MRI. Above what lumbar puncture opening pressure is idiopathic intracranial hypertension diagnosed?
questions.why: The danger is to vision, so visual fields are checked and ophthalmology involved. Weight loss and acetazolamide are the treatment.

questions.q: Which features support a diagnosis of migraine without aura?
a: Nausea or sensitivity to light and sound
questions.why: Two of the four pain features and one of the associated symptoms, over at least five attacks. The distractors describe tension-type headache and cluster headache.

questions.q: A patient has typical migraine with a normal neurological examination. Is neuroimaging needed?
questions.why: Imaging in typical migraine with a normal examination finds incidental abnormalities and nothing that changes care. A red flag or an abnormal examination changes that.

questions.q: In which patients are triptans contraindicated?
questions.why: They constrict vessels. Gepants such as ubrogepant, and lasmiditan, are the acute alternatives for patients with vascular disease.

questions.q: Using simple analgesics on how many days a month, for more than three months, defines medication overuse headache?
questions.why: For triptans, opioids and combination analgesics the threshold is 10 days. Acute treatment is limited to about two days a week, and the withdrawal is treated by starting a preventive.

questions.q: From how many migraine days a month is preventive treatment generally offered?
questions.why: Or fewer if attacks are disabling. Fifteen or more headache days a month for three months is chronic migraine, which has its own options including onabotulinumtoxinA.

questions.q: Which are first-line oral preventives for migraine?
questions.why: CGRP monoclonal antibodies and gepants are now options when two or more oral agents fail, and earlier where cost allows. Each preventive needs two to three months at dose before judging it.

questions.q: Severe unilateral orbital pain lasting an hour with tearing and a runny nose on the same side, recurring daily for weeks. What is the acute treatment?
questions.why: Cluster headache attacks are too short for oral drugs to work. Verapamil is the usual preventive, with an ECG because of the doses used.

questions.q: Which acute migraine drug is preferred in pregnancy?
questions.why: NSAIDs are avoided in the third trimester and ergots throughout. Sumatriptan has reassuring registry data and is used when acetaminophen fails.
